claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been experimentally observed in a hierarchical heterostructured state.
The hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure contains multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Combining multiscale heterostructure descriptors with limited high-fidelity mechanical data will improve prediction accuracy relative to CALPHAD, first-principles methods, and standard machine learning.
The proposed physics-informed surrogate will be more computationally efficient than conventional CALPHAD and first-principles approaches.
Nanoscale chemical-fluctuation patterns and interfacial attributes can serve as predictive structural descriptors for the three mechanical properties.
A limited set of first-principles calculations and targeted tensile and fracture results is sufficient to constrain the proposed predictor.
The HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure provides repeatable nanoscale features that mediate its mechanical response.
Those nanoscale features include alternating phase domains and chemical-gradient interfaces.
Encoding local chemical and microstructural fluctuations allows the model to learn correlations with macroscopic mechanical properties.
Interpolation within a constrained descriptor space reduces the need for extensive ab initio calculations.
The model will predict Young's modulus within ±10% of experiment.
The model will predict yield strength within ±10% of experiment.
The model will predict fracture toughness within ±10% of experiment.
The proposed model will reduce computational cost by approximately 100-fold to 1000-fold.
Traditional CALPHAD, full first-principles methods, and standard machine-learning models often have prediction errors above 20%.
Ab initio calculations are time-consuming and CALPHAD can require significant computing resources.
The surrogate will become unreliable when the tested heterostructure lies substantially outside the training feature space.
Phase transformations, defect-induced microstructural evolution, or extreme temperatures may move the material outside the reliable model domain by changing deformation mechanisms.
Fracture-toughness predictions are especially uncertain because fracture involves complex stress localization.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if mean prediction error exceeds 10% or computational savings are below 100-fold in the blinded benchmark.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires each of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness to be within ±10%, whereas the falsification rule uses an unspecified average error. Individual properties could exceed ±10% while the average remains below 10%, so the benchmark does not exactly test the stated property-by-property claim.
